claim: Intracortical microstimulation (ICMS) in primary somatosensory cortex (S1) has been established as a method of inducing discriminable artificial sensation in nonhuman primates and recent human studies.
source: Pioneering work with nonhuman primates and recent human studies established intracortical microstimulation (ICMS) in primary somatosensory cortex (S1) as a method of inducing discriminable artificial sensation.
evidence: The claim references prior work with nonhuman primates and recent human studies, indicating support from existing literature.

claim: Artificial sensations from ICMS do not yet provide the breadth of cutaneous and proprioceptive percepts available through natural stimulation.
source: However, these artificial sensations do not yet provide the breadth of cutaneous and proprioceptive percepts available through natural stimulation.
evidence: This is a statement about the current limitations of ICMS technology based on the state of the field.

claim: Replicable sensations in both cutaneous and proprioceptive modalities localized to the contralateral arm were elicited in a tetraplegic human with two microelectrode arrays implanted in S1.
source: In a tetraplegic human with two microelectrode arrays implanted in S1, we report replicable elicitations of sensations in both the cutaneous and proprioceptive modalities localized to the contralateral arm, dependent on both amplitude and frequency of stimulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported from the study's experimental data.

claim: The elicited sensations were dependent on both amplitude and frequency of stimulation.
source: In a tetraplegic human with two microelectrode arrays implanted in S1, we report replicable elicitations of sensations in both the cutaneous and proprioceptive modalities localized to the contralateral arm, dependent on both amplitude and frequency of stimulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data showing parameter dependence.

claim: A subset of electrodes exhibited multimodal properties.
source: Furthermore, we found a subset of electrodes that exhibited multimodal properties, and that proprioceptive percepts on these electrodes were associated with higher amplitudes, irrespective of the frequency.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: Proprioceptive percepts on multimodal electrodes were associated with higher amplitudes, irrespective of the frequency.
source: Furthermore, we found a subset of electrodes that exhibited multimodal properties, and that proprioceptive percepts on these electrodes were associated with higher amplitudes, irrespective of the frequency.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The results demonstrate the ability to provide naturalistic percepts through ICMS that can more closely mimic the body's natural physiological capabilities.
source: These novel results demonstrate the ability to provide naturalistic percepts through ICMS that can more closely mimic the body's natural physiological capabilities.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Delivering both cutaneous and proprioceptive sensations through artificial somatosensory feedback could improve performance and embodiment in brain-machine interfaces.
source: Furthermore, delivering both cutaneous and proprioceptive sensations through artificial somatosensory feedback could improve performance and embodiment in brain-machine interfaces.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.

claim: The absence of somatosensation profoundly diminishes a person's ability to move and interact within their environment.
source: The absence of somatosensation profoundly diminishes a person's ability to move and interact within their environment (Cole and Cole, 1995; Sainburg et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Basic behaviors such as walking or reach-and-grasp require substantially greater cognitive load without somatosensory feedback, even with intact vision and hearing.
source: Even with intact vision and hearing, which can provide sensory information about body position, movement, and interaction, basic behaviors such as walking or reach-and-grasp require substantially greater cognitive load without somatosensory feedback.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about sensory integration.

claim: Providing closed-loop motor-sensory control and feedback pathways could lead to vital increases in performance in brain-machine interfaces.
source: Recent advances in brain-machine interface (BMI) technology have led to renewed efforts in this area, under the hypothesis that providing closed-loop motor-sensory control and feedback pathways could lead to vital increases in performance (Bensmaia and Miller, 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Non-human primates successfully incorporated ICMS information to perform discrimination and detection tasks.
source: Non-human primates (NHPs) successfully incorporated ICMS information to perform discrimination, detection tasks (Romo et al., 1998; Romo et al., 2000; Tabot et al., 2013; Dadarlat et al., 2015) and as sensory feedback for brain control in BMI tasks (O'Doherty et al., 2011; Klaes et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior NHP studies.

claim: Non-human primates successfully used ICMS as sensory feedback for brain control in BMI tasks.
source: Non-human primates (NHPs) successfully incorporated ICMS information to perform discrimination, detection tasks (Romo et al., 1998; Romo et al., 2000; Tabot et al., 2013; Dadarlat et al., 2015) and as sensory feedback for brain control in BMI tasks (O'Doherty et al., 2011; Klaes et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior NHP BMI studies.

claim: Recent human studies have provided insight into the feeling and perception of the sensations produced through ICMS.
source: recent human studies have provided insight into the feeling and perception of the sensations produced through ICMS (Flesher et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent human study.

claim: Qualities ascribed by human subjects to ICMS sensations (e.g., 'tingling' or 'buzzing') have been mostly artificial in nature.
source: However, qualities ascribed by human subjects to these sensations (e.g., 'tingling' or 'buzzing') have been mostly artificial in nature (Johnson et al., 2013; Flesher et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior human studies.

claim: It is unclear what range of sensations could be elicited through ICMS.
source: it is as yet unclear what range of sensations could be elicited through ICMS.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Participant FG has a C5-level spinal cord injury.
source: obtained from stimulation in S1 of a single human subject (participant FG, Figure 1; see Materials and methods) with a C5-level spinal cord injury.
evidence: This is a factual description of the study participant.

claim: Current amplitude, not frequency, of the electrical stimulus differentiates the modality (cutaneous or proprioceptive) of the elicited percept at some stimulation sites.
source: We further show that current amplitude, not frequency, of the electrical stimulus differentiates the modality (i.e., cutaneous or proprioceptive) of the elicited percept at some stimulation sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: 96-channel microelectrode arrays were implanted into ventral premotor cortex (PMv) and supramarginal gyrus (SMG).
source: 96-channel microelectrode arrays were implanted into ventral premotor cortex (PMv) and supramarginal gyrus (SMG), and two 48-channel stimulating arrays were implanted into primary somatosensory cortex (S1).
evidence: This is a description of the surgical procedure and is shown in Figure 1.

claim: Two 48-channel stimulating arrays were implanted into primary somatosensory cortex (S1).
source: 96-channel microelectrode arrays were implanted into ventral premotor cortex (PMv) and supramarginal gyrus (SMG), and two 48-channel stimulating arrays were implanted into primary somatosensory cortex (S1).
evidence: This is a description of the surgical procedure and is shown in Figure 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, electrical stimuli were tested across a range of current amplitudes between 20–100 µA with pulse frequency held constant at 150 Hz over an eight-week period.
source: In Experiment 1, over an eight-week period, electrical stimuli were tested across a range of current amplitudes between 20–100 µA, with pulse frequency held constant at 150 Hz (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Stimulation through 46/96 electrodes (48%) prompted at least one response.
source: Stimulation through 46/96 electrodes (48%) prompted at least one response
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: There were 381 reported sensations out of 1229 non-catch trials.
source: there were in total 381 reported sensations out of 1229 non-catch trials (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: There was weak correlation between the number of electrodes that elicited a sensation and the current amplitude (r = 0.34, p=0.42).
source: There was weak correlation between the number of electrodes that elicited a sensation and the current amplitude (r = 0.34, p=0.42, Pearson linear correlation).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was no correlation between electrode impedance and the likelihood of elicited percepts (p=0.80).
source: Additionally, we found no correlation between electrode impedance and the likelihood of elicited percepts (p=0.80, Pearson linear correlation coefficient), pooling all electrode responses over all days.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in the aggregate impedances of electrodes that produced or did not produce percepts (p=0.707).
source: Furthermore, there was no significant difference in the aggregate impedances of either electrodes that produced or did not produce percepts (p=0.707, Kolmogorov-Smirnov two-sample test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: No false positives were reported in any catch trials.
source: No false positives were reported in any catch trials
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data showing subject reliability.

claim: There was no effect of trial history in the proportion of reported sensations during stimulation.
source: we found no effect of trial history in the proportion of reported sensations during stimulation (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The stimulation did not trigger any painful sensations.
source: The stimulation did not trigger any painful sensations
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental sessions.

claim: No adverse events occurred during any of the sessions.
source: no adverse events occurred during any of the sessions.
evidence: This is a safety observation from the experimental sessions.

claim: Receptive fields along the upper arm, forearm and hand corresponded to coarse somatotopical organization in the corresponding stimulation sites.
source: Receptive fields along the upper arm, forearm and hand corresponded to coarse somatotopical organization in the corresponding stimulation sites.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spatial distribution of responses shown in Figure 2.

claim: Of the 46 electrodes with responses, 32 evoked percepts in the upper arm, 18 in the forearm, and two in the hand.
source: Of the 46 electrodes with responses, 32 evoked percepts in the upper arm, 18 in the forearm, and two in the hand (palmar surface of digits and a finger pad).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Stimulation could produce percepts with variably-sized receptive fields in different electrodes.
source: In agreement with previous reports, stimulation could produce percepts with variably-sized receptive fields in different electrodes (Flesher et al., 2016).
evidence: This observation is consistent with prior cited work.

claim: For the majority of electrodes (24/46), receptive fields were reported in the same body region or in the same plane across all tested amplitudes.
source: For the majority of electrodes (24/46), receptive fields were reported in the same body region (i.e. upper arm or forearm) or in the same plane (i.e. anterior or posterior) across all tested amplitudes.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Coarse somatotopy was present between the medial and lateral arrays.
source: Coarse somatotopy was present between the medial and lateral arrays (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is an observation from the spatial distribution of responses shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The medial array was more likely to have reliable receptive fields in the anterior upper arm (46% of medial-array receptive fields).
source: the medial array was more likely to have reliable receptive fields in the anterior upper arm (46% of medial-array receptive fields)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Stimulation on the lateral array induced sensation more frequently on the posterior forearm (51% of lateral-array receptive fields).
source: while stimulation on the lateral array induced sensation more frequently on the posterior forearm (51% of lateral-array receptive fields).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was no clear somatotopical organization within each array.
source: However, there was no clear somatotopical organization within each array as previously reported (Kim et al., 2015a; Kaas, 1983; Flesher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data that contrasts with prior cited work.

claim: The coarse somatotopy found across arrays but not within arrays could be due to the small area of cortex sampled by the implants.
source: The coarse somatotopy found across arrays but not within arrays, could be due to the small area of cortex sampled by the implants, and the fact that the implants predominantly covered upper arm and forearm, areas with a less established somatotopic map (Kaas et al., 1979; Kaas, 1983).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed pattern, supported by citations.

claim: The topography in somatosensory cortex may have been remapped after injury.
source: Another plausible explanation is that the topography in somatosensory cortex has been remapped after injury (Kaas et al., 1983; Florence et al., 1998; Moore et al., 2000)
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to prior work on cortical remapping.

claim: FG reported a wealth of qualitative sensations induced by ICMS that were broadly characterized as cutaneous or proprioceptive.
source: FG has reported a wealth of qualitative sensations induced by ICMS (Table 1). Unlike paresthetic sensations experienced post-injury, these naturalistic responses were broadly characterized as cutaneous (e.g. squeeze) or proprioceptive (e.g. rightward movement), and as being subjectively similar to sensations experienced prior to injury.
evidence: This is a qualitative result from the experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The naturalistic responses were subjectively similar to sensations experienced prior to injury.
source: Unlike paresthetic sensations experienced post-injury, these naturalistic responses were broadly characterized as cutaneous (e.g. squeeze) or proprioceptive (e.g. rightward movement), and as being subjectively similar to sensations experienced prior to injury.
evidence: This is a qualitative report from the participant.

claim: 18 electrodes had cutaneous-only responses across all tested current amplitudes.
source: We found that 18 electrodes had cutaneous-only responses across all tested current amplitudes
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Six electrodes had proprioceptive-only responses across all tested current amplitudes.
source: while six electrodes had proprioceptive-only responses
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: 22 out of 46 electrodes had mixed responses, where the perceived modality varied as stimulus parameters changed.
source: the rest of the electrodes (22/46) had mixed responses, where the perceived modality (cutaneous or proprioceptive) varied as stimulus parameters changed.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Of the mixed-response electrodes, 45% evoked mostly cutaneous sensations, 32% evoked mostly proprioceptive sensations, and 23% had an equal number of cutaneous and proprioceptive sensations.
source: Of these mixed-response electrodes, 45% evoked mostly cutaneous sensations, 32% evoked mostly proprioceptive sensations, and 23% had an equal number of cutaneous and proprioceptive sensations (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The pattern of cutaneous and proprioceptive evoked sensations complements recent reports of multimodal neurons throughout S1.
source: This pattern of cutaneous and proprioceptive evoked sensations complements recent reports of multimodal (i.e. cutaneous and proprioceptive) neurons throughout S1 (Yau et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the findings to prior cited work.

claim: There was a significant difference between the amplitudes that elicited cutaneous or proprioceptive responses, with proprioceptive responses skewed towards higher amplitudes (p=0.039).
source: We found a significant difference between the amplitudes that elicited cutaneous or proprioceptive responses, with the distribution of proprioceptive responses skewed towards higher amplitudes (Figure 3A), when pooling across all electrodes and amplitudes that produced a sensation (p=0.039, Kruskal-Wallis nonparametric ANOVA, χ2(1,378)=4.41, proprioceptive responses N = 79, cutaneous responses N = 302).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was no significant difference in electrode impedance when comparing proprioceptive or cutaneous responses (p=0.237).
source: To assess consistent current delivery across all electrodes, we measured electrode impedance at the beginning of every session and found no significant difference when comparing proprioceptive or cutaneous responses (p=0.237, χ2(1,378)=1.39)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference between the impedance of proprioceptive- and cutaneous-only electrodes (p=0.922).
source: furthermore, we found no significant difference between the impedance of proprioceptive- and cutaneous-only (p=0.922, χ2(1,155)=0.01) or mixed-response electrodes (p=0.372, χ2(1,221)=0.8).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference between the impedance of proprioceptive-only and mixed-response electrodes (p=0.372).
source: furthermore, we found no significant difference between the impedance of proprioceptive- and cutaneous-only (p=0.922, χ2(1,155)=0.01) or mixed-response electrodes (p=0.372, χ2(1,221)=0.8).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: A clear relationship exists between the number of proprioceptive and cutaneous responses and stimulation amplitudes, measured through overall positive slopes for proprioceptive responses and negative slopes for cutaneous responses in bootstrapped resampling.
source: We observed a clear relationship between the number of proprioceptive and cutaneous responses and stimulation amplitudes, measured through overall positive slopes in the 1st-order polynomial fit at each iteration for proprioceptive responses, and negative slopes for cutaneous responses (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from bootstrapped analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Experiment 2 tested a subset of 5 electrodes with robust responses across all tested amplitudes in Experiment 1.
source: Experiment 2 tested a subset of 5 electrodes with robust responses across all tested amplitudes in Experiment 1 (Figure 2B, Figure 3D).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, each electrode was stimulated with five amplitudes (range 20 to 100 μA) at six different frequencies (range 50 to 300 Hz) in a pseudorandomly-interleaved fashion over three consecutive days.
source: In a pseudorandomly-interleaved fashion, we stimulated each electrode with five amplitudes (range 20 to 100 μA) at six different frequencies (range 50 to 300 Hz) over the course of three consecutive days (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for Experiment 2.

claim: The effect of amplitude on sensation modality was reproduced in Experiment 2 when pooling across all responses (p=2×10−5).
source: We reproduced the effect of amplitude on sensation modality, either proprioceptive or cutaneous, when pooling across all responses (p=2×10−5, χ2(1323)= 18.17, Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 data analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was no significant effect on modality due to electrode impedance (p=0.305).
source: Similar to the main mapping task, we did not find any significant effect on modality due to electrode impedance (p=0.305, χ2(1323)=0.8).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 data analysis.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was no significance when testing the effect of frequency in eliciting proprioceptive or cutaneous responses (p=0.22).
source: Furthermore, there was no significance when testing the effect of frequency in eliciting proprioceptive or cutaneous responses (p=0.22, χ2(1323)= 1.48).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 data analysis.

claim: The amplitude-specific effect on sensation modality is surprising given the more commonly observed effect of frequency and pulse-width modulation on sensation in the periphery.
source: This amplitude-specific effect on sensation modality is perhaps surprising given the more commonly observed effect of frequency and pulse-width modulation on sensation in the periphery (Graczyk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing the findings to prior cited work on peripheral stimulation.

claim: There is evidence of tactile and proprioceptive inputs co-modulating S1 firing activity.
source: Although there is evidence of tactile and proprioceptive inputs co-modulating S1 firing activity (Kim et al., 2015b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The authors are unaware of any reported effect of amplitude or frequency thresholding for different sensory modalities in the CNS.
source: we are unaware of any reported effect of amplitude or frequency thresholding for different sensory modalities in the CNS.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Proprioceptive sensations are commonly thought to derive from activity in areas 2 or 3a.
source: Proprioceptive sensations are commonly thought to derive from activity in areas 2 or 3a
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about somatosensory cortex organization.

claim: Cutaneous sensations more likely correspond to activity in areas 3b and 1.
source: while cutaneous sensations more likely correspond to activity in areas 3b and 1.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about somatosensory cortex organization.

claim: From topographical features, the implants are estimated to lie in area 1.
source: From topographical features, we estimate our implants lie in area 1
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical observations.

claim: There is evidence of interindividual variability in the microstructural organization within S1.
source: however, with evidence of interindividual variability in the microstructural organization within S1 (Geyer et al., 1999)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Higher current amplitudes could increase the effective range of stimulation to include sensory areas 3a or 2.
source: it is possible that higher current amplitudes could increase the effective range of stimulation to include sensory areas 3a or 2.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed amplitude effect.

claim: The two implants are well within the arm and forearm regions of S1.
source: Moreover, given the receptive fields activated during stimulation, the two implants are well within the arm and forearm regions of S1
evidence: This is an inference based on the receptive field data.

claim: Arm and forearm regions of S1 might receive a larger ratio of proprioceptive-to-cutaneous signals than hand regions.
source: which might receive a larger ratio of proprioceptive-to-cutaneous signals than hand regions (McKenna et al., 1982)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In Experiment 1, there was a strong positive correlation between intensity and amplitude (r = 0.2, p=2.1×10−5).
source: In Experiment 1, we found a strong positive correlation between intensity and amplitude (r = 0.2, p=2.1×10−5, Pearson linear correlation coefficient)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Sensation intensity was 2.4 ± 1.9 a.u. (mean ±s.d.) for 20 μA stimulation.
source: with an intensity of 2.4 ± 1.9 a.u. (mean ±s.d.) for 20 μA
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Sensation intensity was 4.0 ± 2.1 a.u. for 100 μA stimulation.
source: and 4.0 ± 2.1 a.u. for 100 μA
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: There was a negative correlation between the current amplitude and the standard deviation of the normalized intensity (r = −0.6, p=0.12).
source: We measured a negative correlation between the current amplitude and the standard deviation of the intensity (r = −0.6, p=0.12).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The majority of responses in Experiment 1 were short duration (N = 225), followed by medium (N = 122) with very few long responses (N = 12).
source: The majority of responses were short (N = 225), followed by medium (N = 122) with very few long responses (N = 12).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: In Experiment 2, the trend in duration was replicated (N = 268, 55 and 1 for short, medium and long, respectively).
source: For Experiment 2 this trend was replicated (N = 268, 55 and 1. Short, medium and long, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Experiment 2 data.

claim: There was no relationship between duration of the sensation and amplitude of stimulation (p=0.1).
source: There was no relationship between duration of the sensation and either amplitude of stimulation (p=0.1, χ2(1323)=4.53)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was no relationship between duration of the sensation and frequency of stimulation (p=0.2).
source: or frequency of stimulation (p=0.2, χ2(1323)=2.83).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: This is the first report in human of replicable, purely naturalistic proprioceptive and cutaneous sensations induced through ICMS.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first report in human of replicable, purely naturalistic proprioceptive and cutaneous sensations induced through ICMS.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: Stimulation over a wide range of amplitudes and frequencies generated qualitatively diverse sensations.
source: Stimulation over a wide range of amplitudes and frequencies generated qualitatively diverse sensations
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Percept modality was strongly linked to variations in amplitude.
source: although percept modality was strongly linked to variations in amplitude.
evidence: This is a summary of the key experimental finding.

claim: The ability to evoke proprioceptive sensations could allow the subject to interpret position- or movement-related information.
source: For example, the ability to evoke proprioceptive sensations could allow the subject to interpret position- or movement-related information, as previously reported in primate studies (Tomlinson and Miller, 2016; Dadarlat et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications, supported by citations to prior primate work.

claim: Eliciting cutaneous sensations could improve the ability to deliver richer somatosensory feedback for object manipulation.
source: while eliciting cutaneous sensations could improve our ability to deliver richer somatosensory feedback for object manipulation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: Cutaneous and proprioceptive somatosensory signals have the potential to improve performance and embodiment when using a BMI-controlled external device.
source: Together these somatosensory signals have the potential to improve performance and embodiment when using a BMI-controlled external device.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: The participant FG is a 32-year-old male with C5-level complete spinal cord injury, 1.5 years post-injury.
source: We recruited and consented a 32-year-old male participant (FG) with C5-level complete spinal cord injury, 1.5 years post-injury, to participate in a clinical trial of a BMI system with intracortical recording and stimulation.
evidence: This is a factual description of the study participant.

claim: The subject has residual sensation in the anterior-radial section of his upper arm.
source: The subject has residual sensation in the anterior-radial section of his upper arm, and some residual sensation in the posterior-radial section of his upper arm and forearm, which present as paresthesias.

claim: The subject has some residual sensation in the posterior-radial section of his upper arm and forearm, which present as paresthesias.
source: The subject has residual sensation in the anterior-radial section of his upper arm, and some residual sensation in the posterior-radial section of his upper arm and forearm, which present as paresthesias.
evidence: This is a factual description of the participant's sensory status.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Boards (IRB) of the University of Southern California (USC) and Rancho Los Amigos National Rehabilitation Hospital (RLA).
source: All procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Boards (IRB) of the University of Southern California (USC) and Rancho Los Amigos National Rehabilitation Hospital (RLA).

source: The implant procedure occurred at Keck Hospital of USC

source: and study sessions took place at RLA.

source: All stimuli consisted of biphasic, charge-balanced, cathodic-leading pulses, with 200 µs width per phase, 53 µs interphase interval, and one-second stimulus duration delivered to a single electrode on the S1 array only.

claim: The maximum charge delivered per phase was 20 nC.
source: The maximum charge delivered per phase was 20 nC.
evidence: This describes a safety parameter used in the study.

source: We selected these parameters, and set electric charge limits according to safe ranges shown in ICMS studies with NHPs (Kim et al., 2015a).

claim: One 96-channel, platinum-tipped Neuroport microelectrode recording array was implanted in each of SMG and PMv.
source: One 96-channel, platinum-tipped Neuroport microelectrode recording array (Blackrock Microsystems, Salt Lake City, UT) was implanted in each of SMG and PMv.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure.

claim: Two 7 × 7 SIROF-tipped microelectrode arrays (with 48 physically-connected channels each) were implanted in S1.
source: Two 7 × 7 SIROF (sputtered iridium oxide film)-tipped microelectrode arrays (with 48 physically-connected channels each) were implanted in S1.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure.

claim: SIROF-tipped electrodes have lower impedance than platinum-tipped electrodes and are better suited to stimulation.
source: The SIROF-tipped electrodes have lower impedance than the platinum-tipped electrodes, and thus are better suited to stimulation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about electrode properties.
